analytic.title: Sex determination of three Neotropical canids by high resolution melting analysis

div.p: We describe a fast and reliable genetic method for sexing Neotropical canids by high resolution melting analysis of amplicons obtained by real time polymerase chain reaction. We used a primer set that amplifies a 195 bp fragment of the ZFX and ZFY genes to determine the sex of pampas fox (Pseudalopex gymnocercus), crab eating fox (Cerdocyon thous), maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus), and domestic dog (Canis familiaris). This new method is useful, fast and reliable for sexing of noninvasively obtained samples with low DNA quality and quantity. This protocol could be easily modified to sex noninvasive samples of other canid species.

We designed a method to rapidly and efficiently determine the sex of three species of wide-ranging South American canids: the crab eating fox, (Cerdocyon thous), the pampas fox, (Pseudalopex gymnocercus), and the threatened maned wolf, (Chrysocyon brachyurus) and the domestic dog (Canis familiaris). Different sample sources were tested such as tissue recovered from carcasses, hair, blood, saliva and feces (Table 1). We used canid-specific sexing primers previously described by Ortega et al. (2004) to perform PCR on these samples, and analyzed the dissociation curve patterns generated by a High Resolution Melting channel on the Rotor Gene 6000 Ò (Corbett Research). The differences in the dissociation curve patterns are due to differences in the base composition of the amplicons (Ririe et al. 1997;Palais et al. 2005;Montgomery et al. 2007;Taylor 2009;Smith et al. 2010;Henri and Mouton 2012;Morinha et al. 2013).

We extracted DNA from a total of 93 samples of known species and sex, collected over a 13-year period (1997)(1998)(1999)(2000)(2001)(2002)(2003)(2004)(2005)(2006)(2007)(2008)(2009)(2010)(2011)(2012)(2013) and stored at the Conservation Genetics Laboratory at Departamento de Biodiversidad y Gene ´tica-IIBCE-Uruguay (Table 1). We also included, as experimental controls, a total of 37 fecal DNA that had been previously identified to species by sequencing short fragments of the mtDNA D-loop and/or the Cyt b regions (Gonza ´lez 2005;Mannise et al. 2012), and sexed using the PCR-RFLP method described by Ortega et al. (2004).

DNA extraction from tissue samples were performed following the procedures described in Medrano et al. (1990) with optimizations performed as in Gonza ´lez (1997), and fecal samples using the QIAGEN Ò DNeasy blood and tissue extraction kit with minor modifications to the manufacturer's protocol. We used ZFKF203L and ZFKF195H primers previously described by Ortega et al. (2004) to amplify a short 195 bp fragment of the ZFX and ZFY genes. PCR amplifications were performed in a final volume of 25 ll following the instructions of the Immomix TM (Bioline) and adding 1 ll of Syto 9 as fluorochrome. & Susana Gonza ´lez sgonzalez@iibce.edu.uy an initial concentration of 10 lM of the forward primer ZFKF203L and 10 lM of the reverse primer ZFKF195H, and 30 ng of DNA template. We developed a protocol with three different profiles. We included an initial denaturation step of 95 °C for 10 m and the following cycles: (1) of 95 °C for 20 s, 60 °C for 20 s and 72 °C for 20 s. repeated for 10 times, (2) of 95 °C for 20 s, 59 °C for 20 s and 72 °C for 20 s. repeated for 15 times, and (3) of 95 °C for 20 s, 58 °C for 20 s and 72 °C for 20 s. repeated for 20-25 times. Finally an extension step of 72 °C for 15 m. The HRM step included a 65-95 °C ramp increasing at 0.1 °C per step with a 2 s pause at each step.

We sequenced two individuals per each species for fragments derived from the ZFY and ZFX genes. We retrieved domestic dog sequences from GenBank for alignment and analysis of sequence variation (ZFX AF027765.1 and ZFY AF027766.1). We determined that females from all species were identical and had a unique restriction site for HaeIII. Since both loci amplify PCR products of the same size (195 bp), we isolated the ZFY fragment by conducting a locus specific enzymatic digestion of the PCR products from known males in a volume of 20 ll which contained 10 ll of PCR product, ddH 2 O, 2 ll of NEB buffer (109) HaeIII and 5 U of restriction enzyme HaeIII (New England Biolabs). Products were run slowly ((40 V) in 3 % agarose gels stained with GoodView TM , yielded one Y band of 195 bp and two bands for the X amplicon one of 157 bp and 38 bp. The ZFY fragment was gel extracted using a gel extraction Zymoclean TM Gel DNA Recovery Kit (Zymo Research).

We conducted an analysis of variance (ANOVA) to test if the melting peaks were significantly different in the ZFY-ZFX fragments among species, and from different DNA source types (tissue or feces) (StatSoft 1995).

The protocol designed unambiguously assigns the sex of the 93 control samples and was 96 % effective for fecal DNA (Table 1). As expected, the HRMA, showed a pattern of two melting curves in the case of known sex males and a single curve in the case of known sex females in all of the samples tested (Fig. 1).

The high resolution melting curves for the ZFX of all four species and individuals were identical. The ANOVA results for ZFX melting peaks temperatures were not significant among species (F = 0.14; p = 0.737). As expected, the ZFX sequenced fragments did not reveal any mutational differences for the four species.

The ZFY melting curves were different among species and the ANOVA results showed a significant F value for the ZFY variance (F = 169; p = 0.005). The pampas fox had the same ZFY melting curve pattern as the domestic dog, but the melting curve profiles (Fig. 1) are influenced by sequence variations in the crab eating fox (at position 8 G/C; JQ946321) and the maned wolf (at position 5 T/C; JQ946322). Furthermore we performed an ANOVA to analyze a relatively large number of crab eating fox samples and determined that the DNA sample source type did not significantly affect the melting temperature peaks of the ZFY and ZFX amplicons.

The advantage of this method is fast in less than 2.5 hours is possible to unambiguously determine sex from different DNA sources and quality. Additionally substantial saving of laboratory consumables (almost five times cheaper), and also reducing contamination risk. Moreover, HRMA is a novel and useful tool for performing population genetic surveys using noninvasive sampling methods that focus on fecal DNA for sex determination of native canids (Ralls et al. 2010).
